tagline.text: 127 figures carved in a rock shelter, the Philippines' oldest known art

location.label: Location
location.text: Highland boundary of Angono and Binangonan, Rizal, Colonel Guido Road, Sitio Ibabaw 2

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (paths are slippery in the rainy season)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (transport and snacks, with entry listed as free, per person)

children.text: The Angono-Binangonan Petroglyphs are a prehistoric site where 127 human and animal figures are carved on the wall of a rock shelter. Known as the oldest art in the Philippines and managed by the National Museum, they pair well with a trip to Antipolo.

The Angono-Binangonan Petroglyphs are a low rock shelter on the hills along the boundary of Angono and Binangonan, Rizal. Human and animal shapes are carved on the wall of the shallow shelter, which is about 63 meters wide, about 8 meters deep and up to about 5 meters high. In all, 127 figures have been recorded, but erosion has left only 51 clearly distinguishable. The carved wall measures about 25 meters wide and about 3 meters high, and shapes such as frogs, lizards and humans are described. The site is managed by the National Museum of the Philippines and was declared a National Cultural Treasure under Presidential Decree No. 260 in 1973. One guide describes it as the oldest known form of art in the Philippines. Angono is about
28 km
from Manila, roughly an hour by car. The site is small and an hour is enough to see it, but allow two to three hours to be comfortable once travel and registration are included.

The site was reported to the National Museum in March 1965 by National Artist Carlos "Botong" Francisco, who found it during a Boy Scouts field trip. Excavations led by Alfredo Evangelista followed in October and November of that year and yielded earthenware fragments, obsidian and chert flakes, stone tools and a polished stone adze. The date is estimated at the Late Neolithic or earlier than 2000 BC, and a 2018 study proposed two phases. The older Phase 1 may be the work of Australo-Melanesian (Negrito) hunter-gatherers, and the more recent Phase 2 may be Austronesian. It is also suggested that Phase 2 might even have been carved by guerrillas in World War II. The site was added to the World Inventory of Rock Art in 1985 and is on the Philippines' tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage. In 1996 the World Monuments Fund included it in its preservation projects and helped install drainage and assign a caretaker. Exactly what the figures mean and when they were made are described as unsettled, since scholars differ. Read the on-site explanations as possibilities rather than definitive statements.

The visit may differ from your expectations. To protect the site, it is open for viewing from viewing decks and you cannot get close to the wall, and many visitors say the worn lines make the figures hard to make out in photos. Some also say the site museum is small with mostly printed information. It is better to go understanding this as a place to see for yourself a trace of Philippine prehistory rather than a "showy sight." The site first opened to the public in 1989 and closed for 14 months of renovations and a new viewing deck until it reopened in October 2015.

This guide is for travelers who want to add a prehistoric site to a day that includes Antipolo Cathedral and the Pinto Art Museum, and for people interested in Philippine history. Opening hours, whether entry is open and the registration method differ between sources, so the current status cannot be stated with certainty. One travel listing even says it has been closed since March 2020, so be sure to check with the National Museum's official channels before you go.

The 127 figures carved on the wall of the shallow rock shelter are the heart of the site. Shapes such as humans, frogs and lizards are described, and to protect them they can be seen only from the viewing deck. Do not touch the wall or approach it. The date is often given as between 3000 and 2000 BC. Many spots are worn and faint, so they are hard to notice at first, and you should look slowly using the exhibit explanations and photo materials. To repeat, the date and meaning are not settled, so take any interpretation as one possibility.

The site began with the story of Carlos Francisco finding it during a Boy Scouts field trip in 1965. Excavations that year are recorded as turning up pottery, obsidian flakes and a polished stone adze. Seen with the on-site explanations, it shows that the carvings are not graffiti from one place but traces of prehistoric life.

A new viewing deck was built during the 2015 renovation, and visitors cannot go beyond it. Because of damage from graffiti, the site is closed outside opening hours. It takes time to find the figures from the deck, so look slowly.

Next to the site is the Angono-Binangonan Petroglyphs Site Museum (National Museum of the Philippines – Rizal). It is a small exhibition with excavated artifacts and explanations, and some reviews judge it to be mostly printed materials. Ask the caretaker about the museum. Visitors often sign in at the museum entrance, and entry is listed as free, but a system of leaving an ID is described, so bring identification.
On the way to the site you pass through a tunnel and then walk a footpath. One review says it is about
1.5 km
beyond the tunnel, but sources differ, so check the exact distance locally. Vehicles are described as not allowed into the tunnel.

blocks.title: World Monuments Fund and heritage status

children.text: The World Monuments Fund included the site in its preservation projects in 1996 and helped with drainage and a caretaker. Its history as a National Cultural Treasure and a site on UNESCO's tentative list shows its value. Preservation is described as a joint effort among the National Museum, the Department of Tourism, the World Monuments Fund, American Express and a Philippine real estate company. Graffiti and monitoring problems remain, so visitors' cooperation matters.

Angono has street murals, the Blanco Family Museum, Nemiranda Arthouse, St. Clement parish church and lakeside parks. On the Sunday before November 23 each year, the Higantes Festival parade of giant papier-mâché figures is held. Combined with the petroglyphs, it makes a full Angono day. Angono is described as the hometown of National Artist Carlos Francisco, and you can see his work in the murals around town.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Petroglyphs and the Angono art town

children.text: Leave Manila and head to Angono by jeepney from LRT-2 Santolan Station or by car.
Check at the site entrance whether it is open, register, then walk through the tunnel and footpath to the viewing deck.
Look for the figures from the deck and look around the site museum.
Go into Angono town for lunch.
Look around the street murals, the Blanco Museum and St. Clement parish church.
The site has short opening hours, so it is safer to go there first in the morning.

items.title: Rizal full-day route
items.subtitle: Petroglyphs, Pinto Art Museum and Antipolo

children.text: Look around the petroglyph site.
Have lunch.
Go to the Pinto Art Museum to see the galleries and gardens.
See Antipolo Cathedral and return to Manila.
Take LRT-2 to Santolan Station and board a jeepney to Angono. Jeepneys to Angono are also listed from Cubao and Starmall.
Angono is about
28 km
from Manila and takes about
50 minutes–1.5 hours
by car. From Angono to the site entrance, you continue by tricycle or Grab.
Go to Angono along Manila East Road. The road to the site is steep and winding, so have your brakes checked.
If you have trouble finding the site entrance, ask the guards on the Eastridge side. Vehicles do not go into the tunnel.
One guide gives the trip from Antipolo Cathedral as about
30 minutes
. It is often used as a day route together with the Pinto Art Museum.
From the entrance, walk through the tunnel and along the footpath. The path is uneven, so shoes with good grip are better.
The site has short opening hours and outdoor movement, so the dry season is easier. In the rainy season the path is slippery and moss can grow on the rock.
Weekday mornings are quiet, and afternoons are cooler but said to be busier. On holidays and weekends the line can get long.
Opening hours are generally listed as about 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., so aim to arrive by 3 p.m. at the latest. One listing gives 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., so keep in mind that closing time may come early.

There is almost nowhere to stay around the site, so the usual way is a day trip, staying in Manila, Angono town or Antipolo. Hotel names and rates vary by season, so check recent reviews on booking sites.

Reviews say there is no suitable café close to the site, so it is better to eat in Angono town. Angono town has Filipino restaurants and cafés, and one visitor recommended Cafe Giya. One travel review named Monte Cafe or a Korean barbecue buffet for lunch.

Angono is about 28 kilometers from Manila, so it suits a day trip without an overnight stay. Places such as the Eastridge overlook are described as open 24 hours and good for ending the day with sunset views of Metro Manila. The lakeside park is known for sunsets.
Before you go, check opening hours and closure days on the National Museum's official channels.
Bring identification. A system of registering by group and leaving an ID has been described.
Stay on the viewing deck and do not touch the wall.
Photography is allowed, but do not use flash on the carvings.
The tunnel and footpath are uneven, so bring shoes with good grip and water.
Go in the morning and have lunch in Angono town.
Combined with the Pinto Art Museum, you can see both prehistoric and modern art on the same day.
Carry out your trash and do not scribble on or damage the site.
Opening hours and entry methods differ between sources. One listing says it has been closed since 2020, so be sure to check before you go.
The road to the site is steep and winding, so check your brakes if you drive.
There are comments that the tunnel and footpath are not monitored, so go with companions rather than alone.
Because of graffiti damage, entry is blocked outside opening hours, so arrive within the hours.
People with limited mobility may find the terrain difficult.
The figures are worn and may be hard to make out, so go with the mindset of confirming a prehistoric site rather than with big expectations.
